docs.title: KP – Molecular Genetic Data
docs.text:
This site collects the material for the course: lectures, hands-on practicals, the data they use, and further resources. The practicals run in your web browser on Galaxy Europe, so you do not need to install any software.

  • Getting started

    Your Galaxy Europe account, the Galaxy interface, and how to work with the shared course histories.

  • Lectures

    Slides for the lectures, grouped by topic.

  • Practicals

    Hands-on modules with step-by-step instructions and questions.

  • Data

    The datasets used in each practical and how to get them.

  • Resources

    Documentation and further reading, general and for each practical.

docs.title: Practicals
docs.text:
• NGS preprocessing and quality control: read quality control, adapter removal and quality trimming in Galaxy.
  • The Unix command line: files, directories and text tools in a Unix terminal in Galaxy, from single commands to pipelines on protein data.

The Practicals page lists every practical with its topics and duration.

docs.title: Before the first practical
docs.text:
1. Create a free account on Galaxy Europe and log in.
  2. Read Getting started if you have not used Galaxy before.
  3. Open the practical from the Practicals page and follow it step by step. Write down your answers to the questions as you go.

docs.title: Teachers
docs.text:

Questions about the course material? Ask your teacher during the practical sessions.

docs.title: Practicals
docs.text:
Each practical is a hands-on module with explanations, Hands-on boxes with the steps to run in Galaxy, and Questions to answer as you go. Keep a notebook (paper or digital) with your answers. The answers are discussed in class.

Practical Topics Platform Time NGS preprocessing and quality control read quality control with FastQC, adapter removal with Cutadapt, quality trimming with Trimmomatic, paired-end reads, Illumina vs 454 vs Ion Torrent Galaxy Europe about 3 hours The Unix command line files and directories, paths, inspecting tables and FASTA files, cut, sort, uniq, grep, redirection and pipes Galaxy Europe (JupyterLab terminal) about 3 hours

The data for each practical are described on the Data page. New to Galaxy? Start with Getting started.

docs.title: NGS preprocessing and quality control
docs.text:
Overview

Objectives

  • Inspect basic read statistics and quality profiles with FastQC
  • Identify an overrepresented sequence and remove it with Cutadapt
  • Trim low-quality bases with Trimmomatic and evaluate the effect with FastQC
  • Handle paired-end reads as a Galaxy paired collection
  • Compare Illumina, 454 and Ion Torrent read-length and quality profiles

Time: about 3 hours

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Today we will preprocess several types of NGS (Next Generation Sequencing) data. Preprocessing is the first step in almost any downstream analysis and ensures that we are working with high-quality sequencing reads.

Raw sequencing data often contain issues such as low-quality bases, sequencing adapters, or other technical artifacts. Identifying and correcting these problems improves the reliability of later analyses such as genome assembly, read alignment, and variant detection.

In this exercise we will work with datasets produced using different sequencing technologies and sequencing strategies.

Datasets used in this exercise:

  1. Pseudomonas aeruginosa — single-end Illumina reads
  2. Human — Illumina paired-end reads
  3. Escherichia coli — 454 and Ion Torrent reads

docs.title: P. aeruginosa single-end Illumina reads
docs.text:
Let us start with sequencing reads from a study of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an opportunistic pathogen that can live in the environment and may infect humans. In humans it often colonizes the lungs, where it can form biofilms.

The reads come from a strain that infected approximately 40 patients in Denmark over the last 30 years. During this time the strain adapted to the human lung environment.

In a later alignment exercise (not part of today's exercise) we will compare these reads to the PAO1 reference genome. The PAO1 strain was isolated in 1955 in Australia from a wound and likely originated from the environment.

By comparing the genomes we can investigate which genes may have been lost during adaptation to the human host, assuming that the PAO1 genome represents a relatively close ancestor.

Before performing any downstream analysis we must first examine the quality of the sequencing data.

docs.title: Step 1 — Get the data into Galaxy
docs.text:
All the data for today's exercise are collected in one Galaxy history. You will import that history once and use it for all three parts of the exercise.

Hands-on: Import the data

  1. Log in to Galaxy Europe (create a free account first if you do not have one). Log in before you open the data link: otherwise your copy is not saved in your account.
  2. Open the shared data history: shared data history
  3. Click Import this history (top right, above the history).
  4. In the Copying History dialog:
    • "Enter a title for the new history": replace the suggested title with Preprocessing
    • keep Copy only the active, non-deleted datasets. selected
    • click Copy History.
  5. A blue message confirms "History imported and is now your active history", but the page still shows the shared history. Click the Galaxy logo at the top left (Home) to return to the main page. Your copy Preprocessing is now shown in the history panel on the right. If the panel shows another history, open Histories in the left-hand activity bar and switch to Preprocessing.
  6. Check that the history contains the five files Paeruginosa.fastq.gz, HG00418_A_1.fastq.gz, HG00418_A_2.fastq.gz, GOS1.fastq.gz and iontorrent.fastq.gz, and the paired collection HG00418 ("a pair with 2 fastqsanger.gz datasets"). The history also shows 2 hidden datasets: these are the collection's two files and can be ignored.
  7. Click on Paeruginosa.fastq.gz to expand it. Check that its datatype is fastqsanger.gz. A preview of the first reads is shown below the dataset details.

Tip: Only if the shared history does not work: upload the files yourself

If you cannot use the shared history, download the five files listed on the Data page to your computer and upload them to a new Galaxy history:

  1. Click Upload in the left-hand activity bar.
  2. Click Choose local file and select the files.
  3. Set Type (set all) to fastqsanger.gz.
  4. Click Start and wait until all datasets turn green.
  5. Build the HG00418 paired collection as described in the paired-end part of this exercise.

Note: What does the datatype fastqsanger.gz mean?

Galaxy uses the datatype to decide which tools can read a dataset. fastqsanger means a FASTQ file whose quality scores use the "Sanger" encoding, and .gz means it is gzip-compressed. Trimmomatic only accepts inputs whose datatype states the quality encoding, so the datatype must be correct before trimming.

docs.title: Quality control is an iterative process
docs.text:
Quality control of sequencing data is rarely a single step. Instead, it is typically an iterative process:

  • Inspect the raw sequencing reads using FastQC
  • Identify potential problems (low-quality bases, adapters, sequence biases)
  • Apply trimming or filtering to correct these problems
  • Run FastQC again to evaluate whether the quality has improved

This process may be repeated several times until the read quality is acceptable for downstream analyses such as genome assembly, alignment, or variant detection.

Hands-on: Run FastQC on the raw reads

  1. Run FastQC (open tool) with the following parameters:
    • "Raw read data from your current history": Paeruginosa.fastq.gz (Galaxy pre-selects the newest dataset, so change it)
    • Leave all other parameters at their defaults.
    • Galaxy Europe shows a banner recommending the tool Falco instead. Ignore it: this exercise uses FastQC.
  2. Click Run Tool.
  3. FastQC produces two datasets: a Webpage (the report) and RawData (the same results as text).
  4. When the job has finished (green), click the eye icon on the Webpage dataset to view the report.

Tip: If a job turns red

A red dataset means the job failed. See If a job fails on the course's Galaxy page. Temporary server problems are fixed by clicking Run Job Again and then Run Tool.

Tip: Reading about the tool

While the job is running, scroll down in the FastQC tool form to read the tool's help text.

docs.title: Basic statistics
docs.text:
The first table in the FastQC report, Basic Statistics, summarises the whole file.

Questions

Q1. How many reads are there?

Q2. How long are the reads?

Q3. What is the GC percentage?

Q4. Which quality score encoding has been used? What is the corresponding score offset? (This information is needed when trimming reads or performing alignments.)

docs.title: Quality plots and overrepresented sequences
docs.text:
The FastQC report contains several plots summarizing the quality of the sequencing reads. Look at each figure and check whether any warnings or failures are reported (the icons in the Summary list at the top of the report: a green tick means pass, an orange exclamation mark means warning, and a red cross means failure).

The most important plot is Per base sequence quality. This plot shows the quality score for each base position as you move from the 5′ end to the 3′ end of the reads. The yellow boxes show the range where the middle 50 % of quality values lie, and the background colours mark good (green), reasonable (orange) and poor (red, below 20) quality.

For Illumina data it is common to see a drop in quality toward the 3′ end of the reads. These low-quality bases should be removed because they may negatively affect downstream analyses such as genome assembly or SNP detection.

Questions

Q5. Look at the Per base sequence quality plot.

  • How does the quality change from the 5′ end to the 3′ end of the reads?
  • At approximately which position do the yellow boxes (the middle 50 % of quality values) start to reach into the red zone (below quality 20)?
  • What happens at the last few positions of the reads?

Also examine the Overrepresented sequences table. These sequences are often adapters or PCR primers that remain in the reads after sequencing.

Adapters must be removed because they can:

  • cause incorrect overlaps during de novo assembly
  • interfere with read alignment
  • introduce artificial sequence similarity between reads

In this dataset you should find an overrepresented sequence that FastQC identifies as an Illumina PCR primer (see the Possible Source column).

Record the sequence exactly as FastQC reports it. You will need it in the next step.

Questions

Q6. Which overrepresented sequence does FastQC report? What does the Possible Source column say, and how many times does the sequence occur?

Tip: Copying the sequence

Select the sequence in the FastQC report and copy it (Ctrl+C / Cmd+C). Check that you have copied only the sequence, with no spaces. Cutadapt accepts upper-case sequences only.

Questions: Predict before you trim

Q6b. Based on your FastQC report, which problem(s) should be addressed before any downstream analysis? For each problem, name the FastQC panel that shows it. What do you think the overrepresented sequence is, and in which part of the reads would you expect to find it?

docs.title: Step 3 — Remove adapters using Cutadapt
docs.text:
Next we will remove the primer sequence from the reads using the program Cutadapt. We will search for it in two ways:

  • as a 3′ adapter, which can occur anywhere in the read, including only partially at the 3′ end. Everything from the adapter to the end of the read is removed.
  • as an anchored 5′ adapter, which must occur in full at the very beginning of the read. In Cutadapt a 5′ adapter is anchored by writing a ^ in front of the sequence.

Hands-on: Run Cutadapt

  1. Run Cutadapt (open tool) with the following parameters:
    • "Single-end or Paired-end reads?": Single-end
      • "FASTQ/A file": Paeruginosa.fastq.gz
      • In "Read 1 Adapters":
        • "Insert 3' (End) Adapters"
          • "Source": Enter custom sequence
            • "Custom 3' adapter sequence": the sequence you recorded from FastQC. The box already contains an example value (AATTGGCC): delete it first, so that the box contains only your sequence.
        • "Insert 5' (Front) Adapters"
          • "Source": Enter custom sequence
            • "Custom 5' adapter sequence": ^ followed immediately by the same sequence (this makes the 5′ adapter anchored). Again, delete the example value first.
    • In "Adapter Handling Options": keep the defaults ("Maximum error rate": 0.1, "Minimum overlap length": 3).
    • In "Read Filtering Options" (click the section title to expand it):
      • "Minimum length (R1)": 50
    • "Additional outputs to generate": tick Report
  2. Click Run Tool.
  3. Rename the output Read 1 Output to Paeruginosa.cut: click the dataset, click the pencil icon, change Name, and click Save.

After trimming, reads shorter than 50 nt are discarded ("Minimum length (R1)"). This and the other Cutadapt settings can be changed in the tool form. More information about adapter types can be found in the Cutadapt documentation — Adapter types.

docs.title: Inspect the Cutadapt report
docs.text:
When the job has finished, click the eye icon on the Report dataset. The statistics are shown at the top of the report (=== Summary ===), followed by one section per adapter.

Questions

Q7. How many reads contained the adapter (Reads with adapters)? Compare this with the number of occurrences FastQC reported. If the numbers differ, suggest why. (Hint: look at the length column in the table "Overview of removed sequences" — how long are most of the removed sequences?)

Q8. How many reads were removed because they were too short?

Q7b. Did the Cutadapt result support your prediction in Q6b? What do these numbers tell you about how much of the original dataset was affected by adapter/primer sequence?

docs.title: Step 4 — Trim low-quality bases with Trimmomatic
docs.text:
Next we will remove low-quality bases from the ends of the reads using Trimmomatic. Trimmomatic applies its trimming operations in the order you list them, so add them in the order given below.

Questions: Predict before you trim

Q8b. Look again at the Per base sequence quality plot of the raw reads (Q5). Which part of the reads do you expect quality trimming to affect most? What do you expect to happen to the read lengths, and could some reads disappear completely?

Hands-on: Run Trimmomatic

  1. Run Trimmomatic (open tool) with the following parameters:
    • "Single-end or paired-end reads?": Single-end
      • "Input FASTQ file": Paeruginosa.cut
    • "Perform initial ILLUMINACLIP step?": no
    • In "Trimmomatic Operation", set the first operation and use Insert Trimmomatic Operation to add the others:
      1. "Select Trimmomatic operation to perform": Cut bases off the start of a read, if below a threshold quality (LEADING)
        • "Minimum quality required to keep a base": 20
      2. Cut bases off the end of a read, if below a threshold quality (TRAILING)
        • "Minimum quality required to keep a base": 20
      3. Sliding window trimming (SLIDINGWINDOW)
        • "Number of bases to average across": 4
        • "Average quality required": 20
      4. Drop reads below a specified length (MINLEN)
        • "Minimum length of reads to be kept": 36
    • "Output trimmomatic log messages?": Yes
  2. Click Run Tool.
  3. Rename the trimmed reads (the output named Trimmomatic on Paeruginosa.cut, not the log file) to Paeruginosa.cut.trim.

The trimming statistics are in the log file output. Click its eye icon and find the line starting with Input Reads:.

Questions

Q9. How many reads survived the trimming? How many were dropped?

Q9b. Which of the four operations is the one designed to remove whole reads? Using your answer to Q8b, explain why so many more reads were lost here than in the Cutadapt step.

docs.title: Step 5 — Compare FastQC reports
docs.text:
After trimming, examine how the dataset has changed.

Hands-on: Run FastQC on the trimmed data

  1. Run FastQC (open tool):
    • "Raw read data from your current history": select both Paeruginosa.cut and Paeruginosa.cut.trim. Click the Multiple datasets button, then click the datasets in the list. Galaxy may already have selected one dataset for you, and clicking a selected dataset removes it again: check that the box shows exactly these two datasets (remove any other with its ×). Galaxy runs FastQC once for each dataset.
  2. Open the three FastQC Webpage reports (raw, Paeruginosa.cut and Paeruginosa.cut.trim). Galaxy names each report after the number of its input in your history: for example, FastQC on dataset 1: Webpage is the report for dataset 1, Paeruginosa.fastq.gz.

Tip: Viewing reports side by side

Click the grid icon in the top bar (Enable/Disable Window Manager). Each report you open with the eye icon then appears in its own window, which you can move and resize to arrange the three reports next to each other. When you have finished, close the windows (×) and click the grid icon again to switch the Window Manager off; otherwise the windows cover the tool forms. Alternatively, open each report in its own browser tab: Ctrl-click (Cmd-click on a Mac) the eye icon.

Questions

Q10. Compare the three FastQC reports side by side: before (raw reads) and after each preprocessing step (adapter-trimmed and quality-trimmed reads). Look at the plots themselves, not only the summary icons.

  1. How did the Per base sequence quality plot change after adapter trimming, and after quality trimming?
  2. Is the overrepresented sequence still reported after adapter trimming?
  3. Did the Per base sequence content plot change after trimming?
  4. Which part of the reads still shows an unusual pattern in Per base sequence content? Suggest an additional trimming step, and which tool option could perform it.
  5. Before vs after: did preprocessing solve the problems you identified in Q6b? For each step, say what improved, what did not materially change, and whether the step had its intended effect.

docs.title: Human Illumina paired-end reads
docs.text:
Next we will examine paired-end Illumina reads. These reads originate from a ~40× whole-genome sequencing (WGS) dataset of an Asian individual.

To keep the exercise manageable, the dataset has been filtered so that it only contains reads mapping to chromosome 21.

Each DNA fragment was sequenced from both ends. The file HG00418_A_1.fastq.gz contains the forward (left) read of each pair, and HG00418_A_2.fastq.gz contains the reverse (right) read. The n-th read in one file is the mate of the n-th read in the other file. In Galaxy we keep the two files together as a paired collection, so that tools always receive the forward and reverse reads together and in the right order.

docs.title: Step 1 — The paired collection
docs.text:
Hands-on: Check the paired collection

  1. In your history, click the HG00418 collection. It contains two datasets, shown as forward (the reads from HG00418_A_1.fastq.gz) and reverse (the reads from HG00418_A_2.fastq.gz).
  2. Click « History: Preprocessing at the top of the history panel to return to the full history.

Tip: If you uploaded the files yourself: build the paired collection

  1. At the top of the history, click the Select Items (checkbox) icon.
  2. Tick HG00418_A_1.fastq.gz and HG00418_A_2.fastq.gz.
  3. Open the selection dropdown ("2 of … selected") and choose Advanced Build List.
  4. Under What are you building? choose List of Paired Datasets and click Next.
  5. Under Auto Pairing, check that the two files are paired with HG00418_A_1.fastq.gz as the forward read and HG00418_A_2.fastq.gz as the reverse read, and click Next.
  6. Name the collection HG00418 and click Build.

This creates a list containing one pair. You can use it everywhere this exercise says HG00418; Galaxy then runs each tool on the pair inside the list.

docs.title: Step 2 — Run FastQC
docs.text:
Hands-on: Run FastQC on the paired collection

  1. Run FastQC (open tool):
    • "Raw read data from your current history": click the Dataset collection button and select HG00418.
  2. Galaxy runs FastQC separately on the forward and on the reverse reads. The Webpage output is a collection with one report for each.

Questions

Q11. Use Basic Statistics in the two reports.

  1. How many reads are in the forward file, and how many in the reverse file?
  2. How many read pairs is that, and how many individual reads (mates) in total?
  3. How long are the reads?

Q12. Compare the Per base sequence quality plots of the forward and reverse reads. How does the quality change toward the 3′ end, and do the two mates differ?

Q13. Does FastQC report any adapter contamination (Adapter Content) or overrepresented sequences in this dataset? What does that mean for how we should trim these reads?

docs.title: Step 3 — Trim reads using Trimmomatic
docs.text:
Based on your answers above, we will now trim the paired-end reads with Trimmomatic, using the same quality settings as in the previous exercise.

Hands-on: Run Trimmomatic on the paired collection

  1. Run Trimmomatic (open tool) with the following parameters:
    • "Single-end or paired-end reads?": Paired-end (as collection)
      • "Select FASTQ dataset collection with R1/R2 pair": HG00418
    • "Perform initial ILLUMINACLIP step?": no
    • "Trimmomatic Operation": the same four operations, in the same order, as for P. aeruginosa:
      1. LEADING: 20
      2. TRAILING: 20
      3. SLIDINGWINDOW: "Number of bases to average across" 4, "Average quality required" 20
      4. MINLEN: 36
    • "Output trimmomatic log messages?": Yes
  2. Click Run Tool.
  3. Trimmomatic produces two collections: paired (forward + reverse reads whose mate also survived) and unpaired (reads whose mate was removed), and a log file.

Open the log file and find the line starting with Input Read Pairs:.

Questions

Q14. Record the trimming statistics:

  • Input read pairs
  • Both surviving
  • Forward only surviving
  • Reverse only surviving
  • Dropped

Q14b. Why can paired-end trimming produce these four categories? In this dataset, more forward only than reverse only reads survived. Which of your FastQC observations (Q12) explains that?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Unlike the previous dataset, this dataset contains paired-end reads. Each DNA fragment was sequenced from both ends, producing a forward and a reverse read.

During trimming, some reads may fail the quality filters while their partner read remains usable.

This is why the output contains categories such as:

  • Both surviving — both reads in the pair passed filtering (Galaxy output: the paired collection)
  • Forward only surviving — only the forward read passed (Galaxy output: forward in the unpaired collection)
  • Reverse only surviving — only the reverse read passed (Galaxy output: reverse in the unpaired collection)
  • Dropped — both reads failed filtering

Reads where only one partner survives are no longer paired and are therefore treated as single-end reads in downstream analyses.

Questions

Q15. How many reads in total ended up in the unpaired collection? Could they be used together with the paired reads in a paired-end alignment?

docs.title: E. coli 454 and Ion Torrent data
docs.text:
In this final exercise we will examine sequencing data generated using two older sequencing technologies: 454 pyrosequencing and Ion Torrent.

The reads originate from the German E. coli outbreak in 2011 associated with contaminated cucumbers and sprouts.

Note that these datasets were not generated using Illumina sequencing. In Galaxy they still have the datatype fastqsanger.gz, because the datatype describes the file format and quality encoding, not the sequencing technology. Keep track of which technology produced which file by giving the datasets clear names.

docs.title: Step 1 — The data
docs.text:
Hands-on: Name the datasets

  1. Find GOS1.fastq.gz (the 454 dataset) and iontorrent.fastq.gz (the Ion Torrent dataset) in your history.
  2. Optional: rename them to GOS1 (454) and iontorrent (Ion Torrent) so that the FastQC reports are easy to tell apart.

docs.title: Step 2 — Run FastQC
docs.text:
Hands-on: Run FastQC on both datasets

  1. Run FastQC (open tool):
    • "Raw read data from your current history": select both GOS1.fastq.gz and iontorrent.fastq.gz (Multiple datasets). As before, check that the box shows exactly these two datasets.
  2. Open both Webpage reports.

Pay particular attention to Basic Statistics, the Per base sequence quality plot and the Sequence Length Distribution.

Questions

Q16. For each dataset, record from Basic Statistics:

  • number of reads
  • read length (range)
  • GC percentage

Q17. Open the Per base sequence quality, Per sequence quality scores and Sequence Length Distribution plots of both reports side by side. What differences do you observe in read length, in quality, and in how quality deteriorates along the reads?

Q18. Compare all three technologies you have seen today (Illumina, 454, Ion Torrent). Which produce reads of a fixed length? Summarise, in one sentence each, the characteristic read length and quality profile of each technology. Based on the plots, which dataset would you expect to lose the most reads if trimmed with the same settings as the Illumina data (average quality 20), and why? (You can test your prediction in the optional exploration, Q19.)

docs.title: Optional exploration
docs.text:
Try trimming the 454 and Ion Torrent reads to remove low-quality bases with Trimmomatic (open tool) ("Single-end", the same four operations as before), and then run FastQC again to evaluate the effect of trimming.

Questions

Q19. (Optional) How many reads survive trimming for each technology? Explain what you observe.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
Quality control is a loop: observe → predict → process → observe again → compare → explain.

Questions

Q20. You receive a new sequencing dataset tomorrow. Before any downstream analysis:

  1. What would you inspect first, and in which FastQC panels?
  2. How would you decide whether trimming is necessary, and which kind?
  3. What would you check after preprocessing?

docs.title: Exercise completed
docs.text:
Congratulations — you have now completed the data preprocessing exercises.

You have explored sequencing data generated using multiple technologies and learned how to:

  • inspect sequencing read statistics
  • evaluate read quality using FastQC
  • remove adapters and primers
  • trim low-quality bases
  • compare different sequencing technologies

docs.title: The Unix command line
docs.text:
Overview

Objectives

  • Open a Unix terminal in Galaxy Europe and find out where you are in the file system
  • Create, copy, move and delete files and directories, using relative and absolute paths
  • Inspect a table and a FASTA file with head, tail, less and wc
  • Select columns with cut, combine them with paste, and sort text and numbers with sort
  • Count identical lines with sort and uniq
  • Search text with grep and simple patterns
  • Save output with > and >>, and connect commands with pipes (|)
  • Answer a biological question with a pipeline that you compose yourself

Time: about 3 hours

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Most molecular genetic data are plain text: sequence files (FASTA, FASTQ), alignments (SAM), variant files (VCF), annotation tables and the result tables of almost every analysis tool. The Unix command line gives you small, fast programs that each do one thing with text: show the first lines, count lines, pick out columns, sort, or search. Connected to each other, they answer real questions about data in seconds, and the same commands work on your laptop, on a Galaxy server and on a large compute cluster.

In this practical you work in a real Unix terminal inside Galaxy Europe. You will:

  • find your way around the file system;
  • create, copy, move and delete files and directories;
  • inspect a protein table and a FASTA file;
  • cut, sort, count and search them;
  • connect commands with pipes to answer a biological question.

The slides for this practical are on the Lectures page.

Data. You will work with two files exported from UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot, the manually reviewed part of the UniProt protein database:

  • proteins.tsv: a table of protein entries for a panel of well-known human disease genes (such as TP53, BRCA1, CFTR and HBB) and the corresponding proteins in other vertebrates;
  • proteins.fasta: the amino-acid sequences of the same proteins.

docs.title: Get a terminal in Galaxy
docs.text: You need a registered Galaxy Europe account for this practical: the terminal runs in an Interactive Tool, and Galaxy Europe starts Interactive Tools only for users who are logged in.

docs.title: Step 1 — Import the data history
docs.text:
Hands-on: Import the data

  1. Log in to Galaxy Europe (create a free account first if you do not have one). Log in before you open the data link: otherwise your copy is not saved in your account.
  2. Open the shared data history: shared data history
  3. Click Import this history (top right, above the history).
  4. In the Copying History dialog:
    • "Enter a title for the new history": replace the suggested title with Unix practical
    • keep Copy only the active, non-deleted datasets. selected
    • click Copy History.
  5. A blue message confirms "History imported and is now your active history", but the page still shows the shared history. Click the Galaxy logo at the top left (Home) to return to the main page. Your copy Unix practical is now shown in the history panel on the right. If the panel shows another history, open Histories in the left-hand activity bar and switch to Unix practical.
  6. Check that the history contains the two datasets proteins.tsv and proteins.fasta.

docs.title: Step 2 — Start JupyterLab
docs.text:
JupyterLab is a web-based working environment. Galaxy Europe runs it for you as an Interactive Tool, and it includes a Unix terminal.

Hands-on: Start the JupyterLab Interactive Tool

  1. Check that Unix practical is your current history (history panel on the right). JupyterLab can only fetch data from the history it was started from.
  2. Click Tools in the activity bar, type JupyterLab in the tool search box, and click Interactive JupyterLab Notebook.
  3. Keep the setting "Do you already have a notebook?" at Start with a fresh notebook, and click Run Tool.
  4. Galaxy shows "Waiting for InteractiveTool result view(s) to become available", and three new items appear in your history: JupyTool output collection, Executed JupyTool Notebook and Interactive JupyterLab Notebook. They do not turn green while JupyterLab is running. This is normal.
  5. Click Interactive Tools in the activity bar. Under Active Interactive Tools you see JupyTool interactive tool with the status Running. This usually takes less than a minute. If it is still not listed as Running after five minutes, click Run Tool again (step 3), and tell a teacher if that does not help either.
  6. Click the ↗ icon (Open in new tab) next to it. JupyterLab opens in a new browser tab. (Clicking the name itself opens JupyterLab inside the Galaxy page, where it has less room.)

Warning: Not logged in?

If you start the tool without being logged in, Galaxy still shows a green message, but the new history items turn red and no Interactive Tool appears. Log in, import the data history again, and start the tool again.

docs.title: Step 3 — Open a terminal
docs.text:
Hands-on: Open a terminal in JupyterLab

  1. In JupyterLab, click File → New → Terminal. (You can also click the Terminal tile in the Launcher, under Other.) If JupyterLab asks "Would you like to get notified about official Jupyter news?", click No.

  2. A terminal tab opens with a line like this, followed by a blinking cursor:

    (base) jovyan@4aa74bb55da1:/data/jwd07/pulsar_staging/113469050/working/jupyter$

    This is the prompt. It shows your user name (jovyan), the name of the computer (a random code) and the directory you are in, and it ends with $. The shell is waiting for a command. (base) is the name of a software environment; you can ignore it.

Tip: Typing, pasting and stopping

  • Type a command and press Enter to run it. Commands, options and file names are case-sensitive, and the spaces between them matter.
  • Type the commands yourself where you can: that is how you learn them. To paste a command, right-click → Paste in the terminal (on a Mac, Cmd+V also works). Copy text from the terminal by selecting it and choosing right-click → Copy.
  • Ctrl+C in the terminal does not copy. It stops the command that is running and gives you a new prompt. Use it whenever the terminal seems stuck, for example after an unfinished quote (the prompt changes to >).
  • Press Tab to complete a file or command name, and the up arrow to get your previous commands back.

Warning: This terminal is temporary

Your terminal runs in a temporary environment that exists only while the Interactive Tool is running.

  • Closing the browser tab, or the terminal tab, does not stop it: reopen it from Interactive Tools in Galaxy. In JupyterLab, File → New → Terminal gives you a new terminal in the same environment, with your files still there.
  • When the tool is stopped (the red square in Interactive Tools, or File → Shut Down in JupyterLab), every file you made in the terminal is deleted. The red square stops the tool at once, without asking. Only the files you send to your Galaxy history with put (see the end of the practical) are kept.

Do the practical in one sitting if you can. If you have to start again, the tip Starting again at the end of Part 1 gets you back to work in a minute.

docs.title: Part 1 — Where am I?
docs.text:
Every command line has the same parts: the command (the program to run), then options that change what it does (usually starting with -), then arguments (usually the files it works on), all separated by spaces. In ls -l /import the command is ls, the option is -l and the argument is /import.

The files on a Unix computer are organised in a tree of directories (folders). The top of the tree is /, the root. You are always in one directory, the current working directory.

Hands-on: Look around

  1. Print the current working directory:

    pwd

  2. Go to your home directory with cd (change directory) without an argument, and print the working directory again:

    cd
pwd

  3. List the contents of the directory, first briefly and then in the long format:

    ls
ls -l

Questions

Q1. What does pwd print right after you open the terminal, and what does it print after cd? Which of the two is your home directory?

docs.title: Make a working directory and get the data
docs.text:
Hands-on: Create a directory for this practical

  1. Make a new directory, move into it, and check where you are:

    mkdir unix-practical
cd unix-practical
pwd

  2. Fetch the two data files from your Galaxy history with the command get. It is not a standard Unix command: this Galaxy environment provides it, and it copies a dataset from the history JupyterLab was started from. Each get prints where it saved the file:

    get -i proteins.tsv -t name
get -i proteins.fasta -t name

    Run each get only once. If you run it again for the same file, it prints a long error message that ends with KeyError: 'extension'. The file is still there: continue with the next step.

  3. get saves the files in the directory /import. Look at them there, then copy both to your current directory, and list it:

    ls -l /import
cp /import/proteins.tsv /import/proteins.fasta .
ls -l

Note: Absolute and relative paths

A path says where a file is. A path that starts with / is absolute: it starts at the root, and it means the same thing wherever you are. Any other path is relative: it starts in your current directory. Three short names are useful:

  • . means "the current directory";
  • .. means "the directory one level up";
  • ~ means "my home directory".

Questions

Q2. Is /import/proteins.tsv an absolute or a relative path? What does the . at the end of the cp command stand for? Write the absolute path of your own copy of proteins.tsv.

Tip: Starting again

If your Interactive Tool was stopped, start JupyterLab again from Unix practical (Step 2), open a terminal (Step 3), and run:

mkdir -p ~/unix-practical
cd ~/unix-practical
get -i proteins.tsv -t name
get -i proteins.fasta -t name
cp /import/proteins.tsv /import/proteins.fasta .

If you had already reached Part 4, also repeat its first step (tail -n +2 …).

docs.title: Part 2 — Files and directories
docs.text:
Hands-on: Copy and compare

  1. Make a copy of the table, and compare the copy with the original using diff:

    cp proteins.tsv backup.tsv
ls
diff proteins.tsv backup.tsv

Questions

Q3. What does diff print, and what does that tell you about the two files?

Hands-on: Overwrite a file (on purpose)

  1. Now copy the FASTA file onto backup.tsv, and look at the first three lines of backup.tsv:

    cp proteins.fasta backup.tsv
head -n 3 backup.tsv

Questions

Q4. What is in backup.tsv now? Did cp warn you before it replaced the old contents?

Warning: No undo, no trash bin

cp and mv replace an existing file with the same name without asking, and so does > (Part 4). rm deletes a file permanently: there is no trash bin to restore it from, here or on any other Unix system. Before you replace or delete something, check what it is (ls, head).

Hands-on: Delete a file, and work with directories

  1. Delete backup.tsv, and check that it is gone:

    rm backup.tsv
ls

  2. Make a directory test, copy both data files into it, and list it:

    mkdir test
cp proteins.tsv proteins.fasta test/
ls test

  3. Make a second directory data, move the two files from test into it, and remove the now empty test with rmdir. The * is a wildcard: test/* means "every file in test". Before you use a wildcard, check what it matches with ls:

    mkdir data
ls test/*
mv test/* data/
ls test data
rmdir test

Questions

Q5. Now try to remove the directory data in the same way, with rmdir data. What happens, and why?

Hands-on: Directories inside directories

  1. Make three directories inside each other in one command. -p tells mkdir to create the parent directories as well:

    mkdir -p nested/level2/level3

  2. Move data into the innermost directory, and list it there. Use Tab to complete the directory names instead of typing them in full:

    mv data nested/level2/level3/
ls nested/level2/level3/data

  3. Before you delete anything, look at everything inside nested with ls -R (recursive):

    ls -R nested

Questions

Q6. rm -r nested would delete nested and everything inside it. According to ls -R, which files and which directories would it delete?

Hands-on: Delete the practice directories

  1. Delete nested with everything in it, and check what is left. Your two original data files in unix-practical are not affected:

    rm -r nested
ls

Warning: rm -r

rm -r deletes a directory and everything below it, at once and for good. Only use it on a directory you have just inspected, like here. Never combine it with a wildcard you have not checked. The temporary Galaxy environment does not make this safe: on your own computer or on a server, the same command deletes your real work.

docs.title: Part 3 — Look inside the files
docs.text:
Hands-on: The protein table

  1. Show the first 10 lines of the table with head, then only the first 3 lines, and then the last 3 lines with tail:

    head proteins.tsv
head -n 3 proteins.tsv
tail -n 3 proteins.tsv

  2. Browse the whole table with less. Use the space bar to go down a page, b to go back, and type /DMD and Enter to search for the text DMD. Press q to quit less and get your prompt back:

    less proteins.tsv

  3. Count the lines, words and characters with wc, then only the lines with wc -l:

    wc proteins.tsv
wc -l proteins.tsv

Questions

Q7. What are the five columns of proteins.tsv? What does one line after the first one describe?

Q8. How many proteins are described in proteins.tsv? Be careful: look again at what is on the first line.

Hands-on: The FASTA file

  1. Show the first 4 lines of the FASTA file, and browse it with less (quit with q):

    head -n 4 proteins.fasta
less proteins.fasta

  2. Count its lines:

    wc -l proteins.fasta

Questions

Q9. A FASTA record starts with a header line that begins with >, followed by one or more lines of sequence. Look at the first header line. Which protein is it, from which organism, and what is its gene name? What is P02649?

Q10. How many lines does proteins.fasta have? Can you tell from the number of lines how many sequences the file contains? Why, or why not?

Note: FASTA and FASTQ

In a FASTQ file (sequencing reads, see the NGS practical) every read takes exactly four lines: a header starting with @, the sequence, a + line and the quality line. There you can get the number of reads by dividing the number of lines by four. In a FASTA file you cannot.

docs.title: Part 4 — Columns, sorting and counting
docs.text:
The table has a header line. Before you sort and count, make a copy without it. tail -n +2 prints a file from line 2 onwards, and > sends the output into a new file instead of to the screen.

Hands-on: Remove the header

  1. Save the table without its header line, and check the new file:

    tail -n +2 proteins.tsv > proteins_data.tsv
head -n 3 proteins_data.tsv
wc -l proteins_data.tsv

Note: Redirection with >

Normally a command writes its output to the screen. command > file writes it into file instead. If file does not exist, it is created; if it exists, its old contents are replaced without warning. Never redirect into the file you are reading from: sort proteins_data.tsv > proteins_data.tsv leaves you with an empty file.

Hands-on: Select columns with cut, and combine them with paste

  1. cut -f selects columns (fields) from a tab-separated file. Save the entry names (column 2) and the lengths (column 5) in two files:

    cut -f2 proteins_data.tsv > names.txt
cut -f5 proteins_data.tsv > lengths.txt
head -n 3 names.txt lengths.txt

  2. paste puts files side by side, line by line. Combine the two files, lengths first:

    paste lengths.txt names.txt > length_name.tsv
head -n 3 length_name.tsv

Questions

Q11. What does length_name.tsv contain, and in which order are the columns? Now run cut -f2,5 proteins_data.tsv (scroll up to see the first lines). In which order does cut print the two columns?

Hands-on: Sort

  1. Sort length_name.tsv in two ways, and look at the last three lines of each result:

    sort length_name.tsv > sorted_text.tsv
tail -n 3 sorted_text.tsv
sort -n length_name.tsv > sorted_num.tsv
tail -n 3 sorted_num.tsv

Questions

Q12. Which three proteins in the table are the longest? The two sort commands disagree: which one gives the right answer, and why does the other one give a different result?

Q13. Which protein in the table is the shortest? What is this protein?

Hands-on: Ask the command for help

  1. Most commands describe their options when you add --help. Read the help of sort, scrolling up if necessary:

    sort --help

Note: Getting help

On most Unix systems man sort shows the full manual page. This Galaxy environment is a minimal system without manual pages: man only prints a message. Use --help here, or look up the command online (for example in the GNU Coreutils manual on the Resources page).

Questions

Q14. Which option makes sort reverse its order? Use it to write a command that lists the proteins in length_name.tsv from the longest to the shortest.

Hands-on: Count identical lines with uniq

  1. Save the organism column, and count identical lines with uniq -c:

    cut -f4 proteins_data.tsv > organisms.txt
uniq -c organisms.txt

  2. Now sort the organisms first, and count again:

    sort organisms.txt > organisms_sorted.txt
uniq -c organisms_sorted.txt

Questions

Q15. How many different species are there in the table, and which species has the most entries? Why does uniq -c on the unsorted file give a different, much longer result?

docs.title: Part 5 — Search with grep
docs.text:
grep prints the lines that contain a pattern. Put the pattern in single quotes, so that the shell passes spaces and special characters on to grep unchanged.

Hands-on: Find lines

  1. Print the human entries, count them with -c, and save all the other lines with -v (invert):

    grep 'Homo sapiens' proteins_data.tsv
grep -c 'Homo sapiens' proteins_data.tsv
grep -v 'Homo sapiens' proteins_data.tsv > non_human.tsv
wc -l non_human.tsv

Note: Patterns

grep patterns are regular expressions. Most characters simply match themselves, but a few have a special meaning:

Pattern Matches ^ the start of a line: ^> is a > at the start of a line $ the end of a line: SV=1$ is SV=1 at the end of a line . any single character [12] one character: 1 or 2

The option -i ignores the difference between upper and lower case.

Questions

Q16. How many sequences are in proteins.fasta? Use grep, and remember what the first line of every FASTA record looks like. Does the number agree with the table?

Q17. Count the p53 sequences with grep -c 'GN=TP53' proteins.fasta. Now look at the table: how many entries have an entry name starting with P53_? Why do the two numbers differ, and how do you make grep find all p53 sequences?

Hands-on: Character classes

  1. Compare these two searches for BRCA1 and BRCA2 (the space after the pattern makes sure that longer gene names starting with the same letters are not matched):

    grep 'GN=BRCA[12] ' proteins.fasta
grep 'GN=BRCA. ' proteins.fasta

Questions

Q18. What do [12] and . mean in these two patterns? Do the two commands find the same lines here? How many BRCA1 and BRCA2 sequences are there in proteins.fasta if you also accept lower-case gene names?

docs.title: Part 6 — Save output: > and >>
docs.text:
Hands-on: Collect lines from two searches in one file

  1. Save the human entries in a new file, then append the mouse entries to the same file with >>, and count the lines:

    grep '_HUMAN' proteins_data.tsv > selected.tsv
grep '_MOUSE' proteins_data.tsv >> selected.tsv
wc -l selected.tsv

Questions

Q19. How many lines does selected.tsv have, and where do they come from? What would the file contain if you had used > instead of >> in the second command?

docs.title: Part 7 — Pipes: connect commands
docs.text:
In Part 4 you needed three commands and two extra files (organisms.txt, organisms_sorted.txt) to count the species. A pipe, written |, does this without files: it sends the output of the command on its left directly into the command on its right. You can chain as many commands as you like.

Hands-on: First pipes

  1. Show only the first three FASTA header lines, and count the human entries by piping grep into wc -l:

    grep '^>' proteins.fasta | head -n 3
grep 'Homo sapiens' proteins_data.tsv | wc -l

Questions

Q20. Write the species count from Part 4 as one pipeline, starting from proteins_data.tsv and without any extra files. Add a last step so that the species with the most entries is at the bottom.

Q21. Write one pipeline that prints the entry names and lengths of the three longest proteins, starting from proteins_data.tsv and without making any files. Hint: sort can sort on one column: -k2,2n sorts numerically on column 2.

docs.title: Part 8 — Challenge: a biological question
docs.text:
The same gene in different species is called an ortholog. An entry name such as P53_HUMAN has two parts, separated by _: the protein (P53) and the species (HUMAN, MOUSE, RAT, …).

How completely are the orthologs of these disease genes covered by reviewed Swiss-Prot entries? Answer the two questions below with pipelines you compose yourself. Start from proteins_data.tsv or from proteins.fasta, as you prefer.

Tip: One new trick

cut normally splits lines at tab characters. With -d you choose another separator: cut -d_ -f1 keeps the part of each line before the first _, and cut -d_ -f2 the part after it.

Questions

Q22. Which protein in the panel has a reviewed entry in the largest number of species, and in how many? Answer with one pipeline.

Q23. CFTR is the gene mutated in cystic fibrosis. In how many species of the panel does proteins.fasta contain a CFTR sequence, and which species of the panel has none?

docs.title: Keep a record and finish
docs.text:
Hands-on: Save your commands to your Galaxy history

  1. history lists the commands you typed in this terminal. Save the list in a file, and send the file to your Galaxy history with put, the partner of get:

    history > my_commands.txt
put -p my_commands.txt

    After a few seconds my_commands.txt appears in your Unix practical history, where it stays after the terminal is gone. You can send any other file the same way.

  2. When you are done, stop the Interactive Tool: Interactive Tools in the activity bar → the red square (Stop this interactive tool) next to JupyTool interactive tool. This deletes the temporary environment and frees the computer for others.

Note: What next?

The same commands work on any Unix system: macOS, Linux, or the compute servers where large sequencing projects are analysed, which you usually reach with ssh. Beyond this practical, sed and awk edit and compute on text, and shell scripts save a pipeline so that you can run it again on new data.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: You opened a Unix shell in Galaxy Europe, found your way around the file system, and created, copied, moved and deleted files and directories. You inspected a protein table and a FASTA file, cut out columns, sorted text and numbers, counted identical lines, and searched with patterns. Finally, you connected small commands with pipes to answer biological questions without writing any intermediate files: the core idea of working on the command line.

docs.title: Getting started with Galaxy Europe
docs.text: Galaxy is a web platform for analysing biological data. You run analysis tools from your browser, and the computations run on the Galaxy Europe servers.

docs.title: Create an account
docs.text:
1. Go to https://usegalaxy.eu/login/start and register with your university e-mail address.
  2. Confirm your e-mail address and log in.

docs.title: The Galaxy interface
docs.text:
• Left: the activity bar, with Upload, Tools, Workflows and more. Search for a tool by name in the tool panel.
  • Centre: the tool form or the result you are viewing.
  • Right: your current history, which is the list of all datasets you have uploaded or created.

Every dataset in the history has a colour showing its state: grey means waiting, orange means running, green means finished, and red means failed. Click a dataset's name to expand it. Click the eye icon to view its contents.

docs.title: Histories
docs.text:
A history holds one analysis. Start a new history for each exercise (the + icon at the top of the history panel), and give it a clear name.

For an exercise you will usually import a shared history that already contains the input data:

  1. Log in first.
  2. Open the link given on the Data page.
  3. Click Import this history. In the Copying History dialog, give the copy a name and click Copy History.
  4. A blue message confirms "History imported and is now your active history", but the page still shows the shared history. Click the Galaxy logo at the top left (Home) to return to the main page: your copy is now shown in the history panel on the right.

The copy is yours, and you can run tools in it. You cannot run tools in the shared history itself.

docs.title: Datatypes and collections
docs.text:
Galaxy uses the datatype of a dataset to decide which tools can read it. Compressed FASTQ files with standard quality scores have the datatype fastqsanger.gz. If a tool does not offer your dataset as input, check the datatype. You can change it with the pencil icon, under Datatypes.

Paired-end reads come as two files (forward and reverse). Galaxy keeps them together as a paired collection, so that tools always receive both files in the right order.

docs.title: Running a tool
docs.text:
1. Search for the tool, open it, and fill in the form as described in the exercise.
  2. Click Run Tool. The new outputs appear at the top of your history.
  3. When the outputs are green, click the eye icon to inspect them.

Tool links in the exercises open the exact tool version used in the course.

docs.title: If a job fails (red dataset)
docs.text:
Click the red dataset to expand it and read the error message.

  • If the message mentions the server (for example container creation failed), it is a temporary problem on Galaxy Europe. Click the Run Job Again button (circular arrow) in the expanded dataset, and then Run Tool without changing anything.
  • If the message is about your input or settings, check the tool form against the exercise instructions, correct it, and run the tool again.
  • If it still fails, ask a teacher (see below).

docs.title: Getting help from a teacher
docs.text: If something does not work, you can let a teacher look at your history: open History options (the menu at the top of the history panel), choose Share & Manage Access, and share the history with your teacher's Galaxy e-mail address. Your teacher can then view the history (and copy it), but cannot change it.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Your Galaxy account has a storage quota. Delete histories you no longer need, and choose to delete them permanently to free space.
